resources.whatItTakes: You need real product management experience — ideally 5+ years shipping features at a company where things actually broke and you had to fix them. Startups hiring fractional PMs aren't looking for someone to run workshops; they want someone who can sit in a messy Slack channel, figure out what the team should build next, and explain why to a skeptical founder. You'll need to hold a roadmap loosely, run lean discovery without a research budget, and manage stakeholders who don't always agree on what the product even is. The consulting layer adds another skill set on top: scoping engagements, writing proposals, setting boundaries, and knowing when a client is asking for more than they're paying for.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most people underestimate the sales cycle. You can have a great LinkedIn profile and a polished proposal and still wait 8–12 weeks for a signed contract. The people who quit early do so during that silence — they interpret no response as proof it won't work. The second failure mode is scope creep accepted quietly: a client starts asking for things outside the agreement, you say yes to avoid awkwardness, and six weeks later you're doing the work of a full-time PM for fractional pay. The third is taking on clients whose problems aren't actually PM problems — a founder who needs a therapist, a co-founder dispute dressed up as a roadmap question, or a team that needs to hire engineers before any strategy matters.
resources.theDip: Weeks six through twelve are where most fractional PMs quietly give up. You've had a few good conversations, maybe one small paid engagement, but you don't have a second client lined up and the pipeline feels thin. Your former colleagues are getting promoted and you're writing cold outreach that gets ignored. This is normal — it's not a sign you chose wrong, it's the lag between effort and result that every consulting business has. The people who get through it do two things: they keep one anchor client even at a lower rate to maintain cash flow and credibility, and they publish something — a teardown, a framework, a short post — every single week so that when someone is finally ready to hire, your name is already familiar.

aiPrompts.task: Write a cold outreach email to a seed-stage startup founder
aiPrompts.prompt:
You are a fractional product manager with 8+ years of experience helping early-stage startups ship faster and avoid costly pivots. Write a cold outreach email to a seed-stage SaaS startup founder.

Context I'll provide: [FOUNDER NAME], [COMPANY NAME], [WHAT THEIR PRODUCT DOES], [ONE SPECIFIC PROBLEM I NOTICED — e.g., 'your onboarding flow has 11 steps before a user sees value']

Requirements:
- Subject line under 8 words, no clickbait
- Opening line references something specific about their product or recent news (not generic flattery)
- One sentence on what I do and who I help
- One concrete, specific observation about a product gap I noticed (use the problem I provided)
- A single low-friction ask (15-min call, not a pitch)
- Total length: under 150 words
- Tone: peer-to-peer, not vendor-to-prospect
- No buzzwords like 'synergy', 'leverage', or 'scale your growth'

Write 3 subject line variants and 1 email body.

aiPrompts.task: Build a 90-day product roadmap for a new client
aiPrompts.prompt:
You are a fractional PM helping a startup build their first structured product roadmap. Based on the information I provide, generate a 90-day roadmap broken into three 30-day sprints.

Client context:
- Product: [DESCRIBE THE PRODUCT IN 2-3 SENTENCES]
- Current stage: [PRE-LAUNCH / POST-LAUNCH / GROWTH]
- Team size: [NUMBER OF ENGINEERS, DESIGNERS]
- Top 3 business goals right now: [LIST THEM]
- Known user complaints or drop-off points: [LIST WHAT YOU KNOW]
- Tech debt or known blockers: [LIST OR WRITE 'UNKNOWN']

For each 30-day sprint, provide:
1. Sprint theme (one sentence)
2. 3-5 prioritized initiatives with a one-line rationale for each
3. One success metric to track
4. One risk to watch

Prioritization framework: use RICE scoring logic (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort) — explain your reasoning briefly for the top 2 items in each sprint.

Format as a clean table I can paste into Notion or Google Docs.

aiPrompts.task: Synthesize user research interviews into actionable insights
aiPrompts.prompt:
I am a fractional product manager. I just completed [NUMBER] user interviews for [CLIENT COMPANY NAME], a [DESCRIBE PRODUCT] used by [TARGET USER TYPE].

Below are my raw interview notes. Analyze them and produce:

1. Top 5 recurring pain points (ranked by frequency and severity)
2. Top 3 unmet needs that the product could address
3. 2-3 surprising or counterintuitive findings
4. Direct quotes (pulled from my notes) that would resonate with the founding team
5. Recommended next steps: what to build, what to kill, what to investigate further

Format for a founder audience — they are not researchers. Use plain language. Flag anything where the sample size is too small to draw conclusions.

Raw notes:
[PASTE YOUR INTERVIEW NOTES HERE]

Do not invent quotes or findings. If the notes are too sparse to support a conclusion, say so explicitly.

aiPrompts.task: Create a scope-of-work document for a new fractional PM engagement
aiPrompts.prompt:
I am a fractional product manager closing a new client engagement. Help me write a clear, professional Scope of Work (SOW) document.

Engagement details:
- Client company: [NAME]
- Product type: [DESCRIBE]
- Engagement length: [e.g., 3 months, rolling monthly]
- Hours per week committed: [NUMBER]
- My hourly or monthly rate: [RATE]
- Deliverables we discussed: [LIST WHAT YOU AGREED TO — e.g., weekly roadmap review, bi-weekly stakeholder syncs, user research synthesis monthly]
- What is explicitly OUT of scope: [LIST]
- Communication norms: [e.g., async Slack, weekly video call]

Generate a SOW that includes:
1. Engagement overview (2-3 sentences)
2. Deliverables with clear acceptance criteria
3. Out-of-scope items (to prevent scope creep)
4. Working hours and communication expectations
5. Change request process (how to add work outside this SOW)
6. Payment terms placeholder

Tone: professional but not stuffy. This is a working document, not a legal contract. I'll have an attorney review before signing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking on too many clients simultaneously without a clear capacity limit
commonMistakes.why: Fractional PM work looks like consulting on paper but runs like a part-time executive role. Each client expects responsiveness, strategic thinking, and continuity. At 3+ clients you start dropping context, missing signals, and giving generic advice. Quality tanks, referrals dry up, and clients quietly don't renew.
commonMistakes.prevention: Hard cap at 2 clients when you're starting out. Track your actual hours weekly for the first 90 days. Only add a third client once you have repeatable systems (templates, async communication norms, documented client context) that cut your per-client overhead by at least 30%.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pricing by the hour instead of by the engagement
commonMistakes.why: Hourly pricing creates the wrong incentives — you get paid more for being slow, clients watch the clock instead of outcomes, and you cap your income at hours worked.
commonMistakes.prevention: Scope the deliverables tightly, not the hours. Use a SOW with a change-request clause for work outside scope.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting work before a signed agreement and deposit
commonMistakes.why: Startup founders move fast and assume good faith. So do new fractional PMs. This happens more often than you'd expect with early-stage companies.
commonMistakes.prevention: No kickoff call, no Slack access, no work until: (1) SOW is signed by both parties, (2) first payment is received or a payment method is on file. Use a tool like DocuSign or HoneyBook to make this frictionless. It takes 10 minutes and protects thousands of dollars.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting clients treat you like a full-time employee
commonMistakes.why: Founders often haven't worked with fractional talent before. Without clear boundaries, they'll add you to every Slack channel, invite you to every meeting, and expect same-day responses on weekends. You'll be doing 40-hour-a-week work on a 20-hour contract, burning out while undercharging.
commonMistakes.prevention: Define communication norms in your SOW: which channels you'll use, your response time SLA (e.g., 'within 24 hours on business days'), which meetings you attend vs. get a summary for, and how off-scope requests get handled. Enforce this from day one — it's much harder to reset expectations mid-engagement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping discovery and jumping straight into roadmapping
commonMistakes.why: Every startup thinks their biggest problem is a missing roadmap. It's rarely true. The real problem might be misaligned stakeholders, a broken user research process, or a product that doesn't match market reality. If you build a roadmap on a broken foundation, you'll be blamed for the failure — even though the problem predated you.
commonMistakes.prevention: Spend the first 2–3 weeks in structured discovery: interview the founding team, review existing data (analytics, support tickets, past user research), and map the current decision-making process. Deliver a 'Current State' document before touching the roadmap. This also protects you — it documents what you inherited.

decisionTrees.question: How should I set my rate for a new client?

options.pickIf: You have 5+ years of PM experience, can clearly articulate ROI (e.g., 'I help you ship faster and avoid costly misdirection'), and the client has raised at least a seed round with real budget
options.nextStep: Anchor the conversation on business outcomes, not hours. Ask the founder what a bad product decision cost them in the last 6 months — then price relative to that risk, not your time.

options.choice: Price by the hour ($100–$200/hour) with a minimum monthly commitment
options.pickIf: You're newer to fractional work (under 2 years), the client is pre-revenue or bootstrapped, or the scope is genuinely unclear and you need flexibility to define the engagement as you go
options.nextStep: Set a minimum monthly floor (e.g., 10 hours/month) to ensure the engagement is worth your context-switching cost. Revisit pricing after 60 days once scope is clearer.

options.choice: Offer a paid discovery sprint ($1,500–$3,000 flat for 2 weeks)
options.pickIf: The client is interested but hasn't committed, or you're unsure whether the engagement will be productive — a paid discovery sprint lets both sides evaluate fit with low risk
options.nextStep: Deliver a concrete artifact at the end (current state audit, 90-day roadmap draft, or research synthesis) that demonstrates your value and naturally leads into a retainer proposal.

decisionTrees.question: A client wants me to manage their engineering team directly. Should I take it on?

options.choice: Yes, take it on and expand your SOW
options.pickIf: You have prior experience managing engineers, the additional responsibility comes with a rate increase of at least 30%, and it doesn't push you over your capacity limit for this client
options.nextStep: Amend your SOW to explicitly define the engineering management scope, add a change request clause for future additions, and increase your monthly rate to reflect the expanded responsibility.

options.choice: Decline and refer a fractional engineering manager
options.pickIf: You don't have strong engineering management experience, you're already at capacity, or taking it on would blur the PM/EM boundary in ways that create confusion for the team
options.nextStep: Recommend a fractional engineering manager from your network. Staying in your lane protects your quality of work and your reputation — and the referral builds goodwill.

options.choice: Offer a hybrid: PM strategy plus lightweight engineering coordination, not management
options.pickIf: The client doesn't actually need a full EM — they need someone to run standups, remove blockers, and keep sprints on track, which is adjacent to PM work
options.nextStep: Define exactly what 'coordination' means in writing (e.g., running standups, managing the sprint board, escalating blockers) and what it doesn't mean (hiring decisions, performance reviews, compensation). Price accordingly.

decisionTrees.question: My client's runway is running low. Should I renegotiate, pause, or exit?

options.choice: Renegotiate to a reduced rate or equity component
options.pickIf: You genuinely believe in the product, the team is strong, and the company has a credible path to the next funding round within 90 days — and you can afford the reduced income short-term
options.nextStep: Get any equity agreement in writing with a vesting schedule and cliff. Have an attorney review equity compensation terms — verbal promises at cash-strapped startups are worth nothing.

options.choice: Pause the engagement with a clear re-engagement trigger
options.pickIf: The client has a specific near-term event (fundraise close, revenue milestone) that would restore budget, and you want to preserve the relationship without working unpaid
options.nextStep: Document the pause in writing: the date it starts, the trigger that would restart it, and whether your rate or scope changes when you return. Keep one warm check-in per month to stay top of mind.

options.pickIf: The runway is under 60 days with no clear path to more capital, the team is in distress, or you can't afford to reduce your income right now
options.nextStep: Give at least 30 days notice per your contract, deliver a clean handoff document (current roadmap state, open decisions, key context), and part on good terms — founders who fail often try again, and your reputation travels with you.

resources.whatItTakes: You don't need to be an AI researcher or engineer. You need to be genuinely ahead of most business owners — comfortable inside tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Notion AI, or Make.com — and able to translate that fluency into plain language a 52-year-old operations manager can act on Monday morning. The real skill here is facilitation and change management, not coding. You're helping teams unlearn old habits and build new ones, which means you'll hit resistance, skepticism, and the occasional 'we tried that and it didn't work.' If you can stay patient, curious, and concrete in those moments, you have what it takes. If you need everyone to be excited before you can move forward, this will wear you out fast.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most people who wash out here do it in one of two ways. The first group builds a beautiful curriculum, records a course, and waits for buyers — and waits. AI training sells through trust and specificity, not funnels. The second group lands a client, over-delivers on scope, burns out, and prices the next engagement too low to compensate. The other quiet killer is keeping up: AI tools move fast, and if you're not using them daily for your own work, your material goes stale and clients notice. Selling generic 'AI for business' to anyone with a budget is also a trap — the consultants who stick around pick a lane (legal teams, real estate brokerages, marketing agencies) and become the obvious person for that niche.
resources.theDip: Weeks six through twelve are where most people quietly stop. You've done one or two workshops, the energy was good, but converting that into recurring revenue feels murky. Referrals haven't materialized yet. You're questioning whether your pricing is right, whether your niche is right, whether you're actually differentiated. This is normal and it's not a signal to pivot — it's a signal to go deeper on outreach and to follow up with every past contact more directly than feels comfortable. The consultants who make it through this window are the ones who book the next thing before the current thing ends.

commonMistakes.mistake: Training people on AI tools instead of solving their actual business problems
commonMistakes.why: Clients don't pay for 'learning ChatGPT' — they pay for faster invoicing, fewer support tickets, or better content output. If your workshop is tool-centric instead of outcome-centric, clients feel like they attended a product demo, not a transformation. They won't renew or refer.
commonMistakes.prevention: Start every engagement with a workflow audit. Identify 2-3 specific tasks that eat time or cause errors. Design your training around those exact tasks. Measure time saved, not features learned.

commonMistakes.mistake: Underpricing because you feel like you're 'just teaching'
commonMistakes.why: AI training is change management, not tutoring. You're helping businesses restructure how they work.
commonMistakes.prevention: Price by project or outcome, not by the hour. Anchor your pricing to the value delivered, not your time spent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking on clients without change management buy-in from leadership
commonMistakes.why: You can run the best workshop in the world and if the manager doesn't reinforce AI use after you leave, adoption dies in two weeks. The team reverts. The client blames you. You get a bad referral (or silence).
commonMistakes.prevention: Before signing any engagement, require a 30-minute call with the decision-maker (not just the team lead). Confirm they'll attend the kickoff, send an internal communication endorsing the training, and set aside 30 minutes/week for follow-up during implementation. Make this a contract requirement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building a curriculum once and never updating it as AI tools change
commonMistakes.why: The AI tool landscape changes every 60-90 days. A workshop you built around one tool's features in Q1 can be partially obsolete by Q3. Clients notice when your demos don't match what they see in the actual product. It erodes trust fast.
commonMistakes.prevention: Schedule a monthly 2-hour 'curriculum audit' block in your calendar. Update one module, test your demos, and note any tool changes. Treat your training materials like a living product, not a finished document.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to serve every industry instead of picking a niche
commonMistakes.why: AI training for a law firm looks completely different from AI training for an e-commerce brand. Generic workshops produce generic results. When you specialize, you can charge more, prep less, and get referrals within that industry's network.
commonMistakes.prevention: After your first 3-5 clients, look at where you got results. Pick one or two industries and go deep. Build industry-specific case studies, prompts libraries, and SOPs. Your marketing becomes easier and your close rate goes up.

phases.name: Foundation
phases.description: Document your methodology and train your AI twin

tasks.title: Document your coaching methodology
tasks.description: Write out your complete coaching framework: core principles, common client problems, your signature process (steps/phases), typical advice for each situation, questions you always ask. The more detailed, the better your AI twin will be.

tasks.title: Train your AI twin on Waymaker
tasks.description: Upload your methodology, past content (blog posts, podcast transcripts, course materials), and sample Q&A pairs to the Waymaker Brain. Configure the AI twin with your voice, personality, and coaching style. Test with 20 sample questions.
tasks.deliverable: AI twin trained and responding in your voice

tasks.title: Design your hybrid coaching program
tasks.description: Structure a 3-tier program: AI-only access, hybrid (AI + group calls), and VIP (AI + 1-on-1). Define what clients get at each level, the coaching journey, and how AI and human coaching complement each other.

tasks.title: Create demo content and sales materials
tasks.description: Record a 3-minute video showing the AI twin in action. Create a sales page explaining the hybrid coaching model. Write your launch email sequence (5 emails). Set up Stripe subscription products for all 3 tiers.
tasks.deliverable: Demo video + sales page + email sequence + payment links

phases.name: Launch
phases.description: Launch to your audience and onboard first clients

tasks.title: Recruit 10 beta testers
tasks.description: Offer 10 people free access to your AI twin for 2 weeks in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. Choose a mix of existing clients and new prospects. Their feedback will improve the AI twin before paid launch.

tasks.title: Refine AI twin based on beta feedback
tasks.description: Review all beta tester interactions with the AI twin. Identify gaps in knowledge, wrong tone, or missing scenarios. Update the training data and test again. This iteration makes the AI twin significantly better.
tasks.deliverable: AI twin refined with beta feedback

tasks.title: Launch to your full audience
tasks.description: Send your 5-email launch sequence. Post demo videos on LinkedIn and YouTube. Include beta tester testimonials in all marketing.

tasks.title: Host first live group coaching call
tasks.description: For Hybrid and VIP tier subscribers, host your first group call. Walk through how to use the AI twin effectively, answer questions, and coach on specific challenges. Record for those who could not attend.
tasks.deliverable: First group call hosted and recorded

phases.name: Scale
phases.description: Grow subscriber base and expand program offerings

tasks.title: Build content marketing engine
tasks.description: Create a YouTube channel and/or podcast sharing coaching insights. Each piece of content demonstrates your expertise and naturally promotes the AI twin program. Aim for 2 pieces per week.
tasks.deliverable: Content engine live with 8+ pieces published

tasks.title: Add course library to the platform
tasks.description: Record 5-10 short courses (30-60 min each) covering specific topics in your methodology. Make these available to Hybrid and VIP subscribers. The AI twin can reference these courses in its coaching.

tasks.title: Launch referral program
tasks.description: Give each subscriber a referral link. Offer 1 free month for every 3 referrals. Satisfied clients are your best growth channel — make it easy and rewarding for them to share.

tasks.title: Develop corporate coaching package
tasks.description: Package your AI twin coaching for companies: team access to the AI twin + monthly group coaching for the whole team. Reach out to 10 companies in your network.
tasks.deliverable: Corporate coaching package designed + 10 companies pitched

phases.name: Exit
phases.description: Prepare your AI twin coaching business for sale, acquisition, or hands-off operation

tasks.title: Document all SOPs for buyer handoff
tasks.description: Create comprehensive standard operating procedures covering every repeatable process in your AI twin coaching business — client onboarding, delivery workflows, billing, and support. A buyer needs to run this without you.
tasks.deliverable: Complete SOP handbook with video walkthroughs

tasks.title: Calculate business valuation
tasks.description: Record the questions this step raises for your business, location, and circumstances. Confirm requirements and assumptions with current official sources and a qualified professional before acting.

tasks.title: Prepare data room
tasks.description: Organize all financial records, contracts, customer data, IP documentation, and legal documents into a virtual data room that a buyer or their advisor can review.

tasks.title: Reduce owner dependency
tasks.description: Identify every area where the business depends on you personally. Delegate, automate, or document each one. Test by taking 2 weeks off and measuring impact.

tasks.title: List or approach acquirers
tasks.description: Create a teaser document (blind profile) for your AI twin coaching business and either list on marketplaces (Acquire.com, Flippa, Quiet Light) or reach out directly to 5-10 potential acquirers.
